title: The Book of Romans
description: Read Paul's letter to the church in Rome one chapter at a time: the gospel of God's righteousness, received by faith, and the life it creates.
objectives: Follow the argument of Romans from beginning to end
Understand what Paul means by righteousness, faith and grace
See how the gospel shapes everyday life and the church

sessions.title: The gospel of God
sessions.intro: Paul introduces himself to a church he has not yet visited and states the theme of the letter (1:16-17) before describing humanity's turning away from God.

supporting.note: The letter's theme in the original language

questions.text: How does Paul describe himself and the gospel in verses 1-6?
According to verses 16-17, what is revealed in the gospel, and how is it received?
In verses 18-32, what does Paul say people did with what they knew about God?
Paul says he is 'not ashamed of the gospel'. What does that phrase suggest about how the gospel was viewed?

sessions.title: God judges impartially
sessions.intro: Paul turns to those who judge others, and then to his own people, showing that knowing God's law does not place anyone beyond God's judgement.

questions.text: What warning does Paul give in verses 1-4 to the person who judges others?
What does verse 11 say about God, and how does the rest of the chapter illustrate it?
Who is Paul addressing from verse 17 onwards, and what are they relying on?
What does Paul mean by circumcision 'of the heart, by the Spirit' (verse 29)?

sessions.title: Righteousness through faith
sessions.intro: Paul concludes that all people, Jew and Gentile, are under sin, and then announces 'but now' — God's righteousness given through faith in Jesus Christ.

questions.text: What conclusion does Paul reach in verses 9-20?
In verses 21-26, how is God's righteousness made known, and to whom is it given?
Verse 26 says God is both 'just' and 'the justifier'. How does the death of Jesus make both true?
What does verse 27 say happens to boasting, and why?

sessions.title: Abraham believed God
sessions.intro: Paul shows from Genesis that Abraham was counted righteous through faith, before circumcision and apart from the law.

questions.text: Why does Paul turn to Abraham at this point in his argument?
According to verses 9-12, when was Abraham counted righteous — before or after circumcision? Why does that matter?
How do verses 18-21 describe Abraham's faith?
Verses 23-25 say these words were written 'for us also'. What connects Abraham's faith with faith in Jesus?

sessions.title: Peace with God
sessions.intro: Paul describes what justification brings — peace, access, hope — and then compares Adam and Christ.

questions.text: List what verses 1-5 say believers now have through Jesus.
What does verse 8 show about God's love, and when was it shown?
In verses 12-21, what came through Adam, and what came through Christ?
Paul links suffering with hope in verses 3-5. How does he describe that process?

sessions.title: Dead to sin, alive to God
sessions.intro: Paul answers an objection: if grace abounds, should we keep sinning? He explains what union with Christ in his death and resurrection means.

questions.text: What question is Paul answering in verse 1, and why might someone ask it after chapter 5?
What does baptism picture in verses 3-5?
What does Paul tell believers to 'count' or 'consider' in verse 11?
Compare the 'wages' and the 'gift' in verse 23. What is the difference between them?

sessions.title: The law and the struggle with sin
sessions.intro: Paul explains the believer's release from the law and describes, in the first person, the inner conflict between knowing what is good and doing it.

questions.text: What illustration does Paul use in verses 1-4, and what point does it make?
According to verses 7-12, is the law itself sinful? What does Paul say the law does?
Christians have read verses 14-25 in different ways (Paul before or after faith in Christ). What details in the passage do readers point to?
How does the chapter end (verses 24-25), and where does Paul look for rescue?

sessions.title: Life in the Spirit
sessions.intro: There is now no condemnation for those in Christ Jesus. Paul describes the Spirit's work, the hope of creation and the love of God that nothing can separate us from.

questions.text: What does verse 1 declare, and what reason do verses 2-4 give for it?
What does the Spirit do for believers according to verses 14-17 and 26-27?
In verses 18-25, what is creation waiting for?
Make a list of the things in verses 35-39 that cannot separate believers from God's love.

sessions.title: God's purposes and Israel
sessions.intro: Paul expresses deep grief for his own people and begins three chapters on how God's promises to Israel stand.

questions.text: How does Paul describe his feelings for Israel in verses 1-5?
What question lies behind verse 6 ('it is not as though the word of God has failed')?
What examples from Israel's history does Paul use in verses 6-18, and what do they show about God's mercy?
According to verses 30-32, how did Gentiles obtain righteousness, and why did Israel not obtain it?

sessions.title: Everyone who calls on the Lord
sessions.intro: Paul explains that righteousness comes by faith, and that the message must be heard and proclaimed.

questions.text: What does Paul pray for in verse 1?
According to verses 9-10, what is involved in being saved?
Trace the chain of questions in verses 14-15. What is needed for people to call on the Lord?
Verse 12 says there is 'no difference' between Jew and Greek. What is the basis for that?

sessions.title: The olive tree and God's mercy
sessions.intro: Paul insists God has not rejected his people, uses the image of an olive tree, and ends in praise.

questions.text: What evidence does Paul give in verses 1-6 that God has not rejected his people?
What does the olive tree illustration (verses 17-24) teach Gentile believers?
What warning against pride does Paul give in verses 18-22?
How do verses 33-36 respond to everything Paul has explained in chapters 9-11?

sessions.title: A living sacrifice
sessions.intro: 'Therefore' — after eleven chapters about God's mercy, Paul describes the life that responds to it, in the body of Christ and toward everyone.

questions.text: Verse 1 begins with 'therefore' and 'in view of God's mercy'. What has Paul shown about God's mercy in the earlier chapters?
What does it mean to be transformed 'by the renewing of your mind' (verse 2)?
What picture of the church does Paul use in verses 4-8?
Verses 17-21 describe how to respond to evil. Which of these instructions stands out to you, and why?

sessions.title: Authorities, love and the day ahead
sessions.intro: Paul writes about governing authorities, sums up the commandments in love, and urges readiness because the day is near.

questions.text: Paul wrote this under Roman rule. What does he say about the purpose of governing authorities in verses 1-7?
According to verses 8-10, how does love fulfil the law?
What does Paul say about time in verses 11-12?
What does it mean to 'clothe yourselves with the Lord Jesus Christ' (verse 14)?

sessions.title: Welcoming one another
sessions.intro: Paul addresses disagreements in the church over food and special days, and how believers with different convictions should treat each other.

questions.text: What were the believers in Rome disagreeing about in verses 2-6?
Why, according to verses 7-12, should believers not judge one another on these matters?
What does Paul say the kingdom of God is (and is not) in verse 17?
Verse 19 says to pursue what leads to peace and building one another up. What might that look like where you are?

sessions.title: Christ's welcome and Paul's mission
sessions.intro: Paul points to Christ's example of welcoming others, then shares his travel plans and asks for prayer.

questions.text: Whose example does Paul point to in verses 3 and 7?
What do the Old Testament quotations in verses 9-12 have in common?
What are Paul's plans in verses 22-29, and what is the collection for Jerusalem?
What does Paul ask the Romans to pray for in verses 30-32?

sessions.title: Greetings and a final doxology
sessions.intro: Paul greets many people by name, warns against those who cause division, and closes in praise to God.

questions.text: Look through the names in verses 1-16. What do you notice about the people Paul greets and how he describes them?
What warning does Paul give in verses 17-20?
What does the final doxology (verses 25-27) say about the gospel and its purpose?
Looking back over the whole letter, what has Romans shown you about the gospel?
